summary: Suggests a method for personal computers and workstations to dynamically access mail from a mailbox server, called IMAP version 2. It obsoletes RFC 1064. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: IMAP2 lets a computer read and manage mail that stays on a server. A client can search for messages and retrieve only the information it needs.

questions: how does imap2 differ from pop
subtitle: A protocol for reading and managing mail stored on a mailbox server.

tldr.problem: Personal computers and workstations may not reliably receive, store, or back up mail, and users may need access from different machines.
tldr.mechanism: IMAP2 keeps the mailbox on a server and lets clients select mailboxes, fetch message data, search, change flags, copy messages, and remove deleted messages.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1176 is Experimental and obsoletes RFC 1064. It describes mail access, not sending mail, which it leaves to protocols such as SMTP.

today: RFC 1176 is an Experimental protocol specification that obsoletes RFC 1064. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Mail Stays on a Server
sections.content:
The Interactive Mail Access Protocol, Version 2 (IMAP2) lets a workstation or personal computer access a mailbox held by a server. The RFC explains that individual computers may be unavailable, difficult to back up, or hard to manage as mail systems.

The server stores the mailbox and lets clients access it from different locations. IMAP2 reads and manages mail; sending mail is handled by a mail transfer protocol such as SMTP. The protocol assumes a reliable data stream and uses TCP port 143 when TCP is used.
sections.plainLanguage: IMAP2 keeps the mailbox on a server that a user can reach from different computers. It manages stored mail but does not send outgoing mail.

sections.title: How IMAP2 Differs from POP and DMSP
sections.content:
The memo describes IMAP2 as a functional superset of the Post Office Protocols (POP2 and POP3). Unlike the POP protocols discussed here, IMAP2 can search messages on the server and return a structured envelope with information such as sender and subject.

IMAP2 keeps mailbox state on the server and does not retain client state between TCP connections. The RFC contrasts this with DMSP, which keeps some shared state with registered clients. IMAP2 is described as primarily an online system.
sections.plainLanguage: IMAP2 can search and describe messages on the server, so a client need not download every message first. The server keeps the mailbox state between client connections.

sections.title: Tagged Commands and Server Updates
sections.content:
IMAP2 carries client commands and server responses over a reliable stream. Each command begins with a unique tag, and its completion response repeats that tag. The server can also send unsolicited data with the reserved asterisk tag; a plus sign tells the client that the server is ready for literal text.

The server greets the client when the connection opens. After identity is established, the client selects a mailbox; no mailbox is selected by default, and INBOX names the user's primary mailbox. Clients can send more commands without waiting for each reply, but a command is complete only when its matching tagged response arrives.
sections.plainLanguage: Every command has a tag, and the server uses the same tag to report completion. It can also send mailbox updates that the client did not request.

sections.title: Fetching, Searching, and Changing Messages
sections.content:
FETCH can return message flags, internal date, size, a parsed envelope, headers, body text, or the full message. SEARCH finds messages matching criteria such as sender, subject, date, body text, or flags. STORE changes message flags, and COPY copies messages to another mailbox.

Deleting a message first sets its DELETED flag. EXPUNGE then removes messages with that flag and sends unsolicited responses as message numbers change. The five system flags are RECENT, SEEN, ANSWERED, FLAGGED, and DELETED.
sections.plainLanguage: A client can ask the server for message details, search by message content or status, and change flags. Deletion is completed later with EXPUNGE.

sections.title: A Typical Mail Session
sections.content:
The RFC's example opens a connection, logs in, selects INBOX, and fetches message summaries for a menu. The client then fetches the body of one message, marks it deleted, expunges it, and logs out.

The server uses OK for successful command completion, NO for an unsuccessful command, and BAD for faulty client protocol. On logout, it sends BYE before the tagged OK response.
sections.plainLanguage: A session can select a mailbox, fetch a message, mark it for deletion, remove it, and then close the connection. Each command's tagged reply shows its result.
